title: A Life That Looks Successful but Feels Empty

reels.hook: The meeting went well. The flat looks right.
reels.hook_b: Everything went right today. So why does it feel like this?
cards: The meeting went well. The flat looks right.
The photos look like the life you aimed for.
Then the evening goes quiet, and something doesn't add up.
Graduates who reached wealth and image goals weren't happier a year later.
Study: Niemiec, Ryan & Deci, J. Res. Personality (2009)
Those who grew closer to people and grew as people were.
The emptiness isn't ingratitude. It's information.
Send it to someone whose life looks great.

reels.evidence: Tier 1 study (N52, 147 graduates); format D, no advice
reels.caption:
A life can look right from outside and feel empty from inside.

In one study, 147 graduates who made progress on wealth, fame and image goals didn't report more wellbeing a year later, and showed more signs of stress. Those who made progress on relationships and personal growth did report more.

What would you keep if nobody could see your life from outside?

Evidence: Niemiec, Ryan & Deci (2009), a small, well-educated sample. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: When did you last feel full rather than successful?

reels.hook: Would you be happier living somewhere sunnier?
reels.hook_b: Why other people's lives always look better than they feel.
cards: Would you be happier living somewhere sunnier?

ONE READING
Obviously. Better weather, better life.

THE OTHER
You'd notice the sun for a month. Then you'd just live there.
Students in California and the Midwest were equally satisfied with life.
We judge lives by what's visible. We live them by what isn't.
What are you judging your life by? Comment.
reels.visual: V1 + grain (Slate), or V3 window with low winter sun (tag window-sun).

source.author: Schkade & Kahneman
source.work: Does living in California make people happy? (Psych. Science 9(5))

reels.caption:
Almost 2,000 students in the Midwest and Southern California rated their lives. Everyone expected Californians to be happier. Californians liked their weather a lot more, but their overall life satisfaction was the same.

The researchers called it a focusing illusion: we give the visible, distinctive parts of a life far more weight than they have in the living of it. We do it to our own lives too.

What are you judging yours by?

Evidence: Schkade & Kahneman (1998). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

carousel_caption:
We judge lives, our own included, by what can be seen from outside. That's a well-documented mistake.

And reaching the visible goals doesn't always feed us. In one study, graduates who achieved wealth and image goals weren't happier a year later; those who grew closer to people were.

What's on your Tuesday-evening ledger?

Evidence: Schkade & Kahneman 1998; Niemiec, Ryan & Deci 2009. Philosophy: Aristotle, NE I.5 (Ross). Idea: Tolstoy.
notes: Everyone expected students in California to be happier than students in the Midwest. They liked their weather much more. Their overall life satisfaction was the same. We judge lives by their most visible features, and we often do it to ourselves.

Aristotle on money, written about 2,300 years ago: wealth is 'merely useful and for the sake of something else'. The empty successful life is often one organised around things that are for something else, with the something else left out.
Two lists. On the left, what your life looks like from outside. On the right, what a normal Tuesday evening actually holds. The gap between them is worth an hour of your attention this week.
